MONROE, La. — After hearing testimony from a neighbor who said his conscience stopped him from draining a dead woman’s bank account, a lead detective who matched phone records to withdrawals one by one, and a battle of cell phone experts that ultimately changed little, both the state and defense rested their cases in the trial of Quinton Tellis Friday.

Tellis is charged with the murder of Ming Chen “Mandy” Hsiao, who had just finished graduate school in July of 2015 when it appears she was tortured to death, stabbed 31 times. Prosecutors spent the last three days and another week in March building a case that weaves together cell phone tower data, bank records and witness accounts into a portrait of a man who they say killed a woman he just met and then methodically attempted to empty her bank accounts in the days that followed.

Closing arguments are scheduled for Thursday before Judge Larry Jefferson, who is presiding over the bench trial. Whether Jefferson will issue a ruling that same day remains unclear.

“A Better Conscience”

Perhaps the most vivid testimony of the day came from Mohammed Mahrous, who lived next door to Tellis’s mother in law on Filhol Avenue in Monroe in 2015. Mahrous, who is currently serving time in Texas on a drug conviction, told the court that one morning Tellis knocked on his door and handed him a debit card with a sticky note on the back.

The note had a PIN number on it, Mahrous said. It started with a 7.

Tellis wanted him to go to the Chase Bank on Highway 165 and withdraw $2,500 in increments of $500 at a time. He said Tellis told him if he brought the money back, he’d be paid for his trouble. Mahrous told the court that the card had an Asian name on it, and a last name that started with an H. It didn’t belong to anyone he knew, and he didn’t recogize the name.

He drove to the bank. ATM photographs entered into evidence placed him there on the morning of July 30, 2015, which was the morning after authorities say evidence shows Hsiao was killed. The photos show he pulled up to the machine and checked the balance. Then, he said, something stopped him.

“A better conscience came to me and told me not to do it,” Mahrous told the court.

Instead of making the withdrawals, he checked the account balance and drove back to return the card to Tellis. He said Tellis got aggressive, calling him a vulgar name, told him he was weak, and told him to give the card to his girlfriend so she could do it instead. Mahrous refused, and told the court he never saw it again.

Monroe police came to his home that fall. He gave a recorded statement, signed a Miranda waiver on September 22, 2015, and submitted to a search of his home, vehicle, cell phone, laptop and DNA.

Tellis, he said, never mentioned the name Mandy or Ming Hsiao.

The defense offered no cross-examination of Mahrous.

Cookson back on the stand

The afternoon belonged to Detective Duane Cookson, the lead investigator in the case, whose testimony walked the court through the physical evidence at the crime scene, the long arc of the investigation, and the painstaking work that ultimately led to a first-degree murder charge.

Cookson was among the first officers at the scene. He found Hsiao’s green iPhone in a blue case approximately three feet from her body, alongside the bed where she lay at the foot. Her hands had blood on them. Cookson said he noticed almost instantly that the phone did not.

When processing the phone, investigators faced a choice between fingerprinting or swabbing for DNA, Cookson said, and since the phone wasn’t bloody, they chose fingerprints but found none belonging to the victim or anyone else.

When detectives searched the apartment on August 8th, they found no cash anywhere inside, not even the $20 that Chase Bank records showed had been withdrawn from Hsiao’s account. That absence took on greater significance after Tellis’s interviews, in which he claimed to have given Hsiao $50 for Lortabs, $25 for a television, and $15 toward a prescription. None of that cash was recovered. The prescription, investigators had learned, was paid by card.

The financial trail Cookson laid out was methodical and thorough. On August 1st, Tellis’s cell phone was placed by cell records in Vicksburg, which was a fact Tellis himself later admitted. During the early morning hours of that date, three transactions were attempted on Hsiao’s Chase account at a Regions Bank ATM. The first was an $800 withdrawal that was declined, then a $400 withdrawal that went through, and another $400 attempt that was declined. Tellis had denied making the withdrawals, even though he could be seen on ATM camera.

On August 7th, his phone called Chase Bank at 11:21 in the morning. That same day, Hsiao’s debit card was used at an Exxon station for $17. When confronted, Tellis produced a new explanation: a man named Kenny whom he described as Hsiao’s “crackhead boyfriend” had been in the car with him and paid for the gas. He had never mentioned Kenny in his August 11th interview, just four days after the transaction. He could not provide Kenny’s last name, address or phone number at the time.

The August 18th and 19th ATM withdrawals from Hsiao’s account brought a new name: “Jay.” Tellis claimed Jay had instructed him to make the withdrawals and paid him in marijuana for his trouble. Investigators had him call Jay right there in the interview room and set up a drug purchase.

Monroe police arrested the man who showed up, and identified him as Termar Key. Key handed over his phone voluntarily, consented to a vehicle search, and had no contact of any kind with Hsiao or her bank accounts. Cookson excluded him as a suspect.

A third name surfaced when Eric Hill, later identified as a cousin of Tellis’s wife, Chiquita Jackson, came to the police station on August 28th and named Curtis Lemons as a suspect. Cookson said he took the tip seriously enough to execute a no-knock warrant on Lemons’s residence within hours. Nothing connecting Lemons to the case was found. Hill later recanted, putting the story squarely on Tellis.

Through it all, Cookson said, Tellis had never once raised either Kenny or Curtis Lemons during his August 11th interview. Both names only appeared after investigators began confronting him with evidence.

The murder charge itself came together slowly. Tellis was initially arrested after his August 19th and 20th interviews only on charges of unauthorized use of an access card and marijuana possession. Cookson testified candidly that he did not yet have probable cause for murder. It was only after he received records from Chase Bank and AT&T and began manually comparing them by cross-referencing every call Tellis’s phone made to Chase with every subsequent transaction on Hsiao’s account that the pattern became undeniable.

Every Chase call preceded a withdrawal, usually within minutes. And before July 29, 2015, Tellis had never called Chase Bank once.

The battle of the experts

Friday morning opened the cross-examination of digital forensics detective Andy Stadius and then testimony from Michael Fegley, a geolocation and cell phone mapping expert called by the defense to challenge the conclusions of Monroe Police Department.

Fegley used a different mapping program than Stadius. It is a controversial system called TRAX, produced by LexisNexis, which generates a different visual representation of cell tower coverage. Where Stadius’s maps showed the familiar wedge shape representing a tower’s sector coverage, Fegley’s program produced what he described as a horizontal plane representation.

The visual difference, however, did not translate into a substantive one. When pressed, Fegley acknowledged that both programs were working from the same AT&T data, the same tower locations, the same sector information, the same location reports.

“My mapping would not conflict with his,” Fegley told the court.

Fegley argued that two location estimates produced during the critical 8:16 to 8:18 p.m. window when calls were made to Chase Bank back-to-back from Hsiao’s phone and then Tellis’s phone on July 29th were geographically inconsistent with each other. He said the distance between them too great to travel in the 25 seconds between reports, meaning at least one of the location estimates must be inaccurate.

But he could not place Tellis’s phone somewhere away from the scene, and he confirmed he was confident the device was in Monroe during the time in question.

The state had also prepared ATF agent Mark Sonnenbecker as an additional cell mapping expert, but after Fegley’s testimony Assistant District Attorney Holly Jones told the court his evidence would be cumulative. He was acknowledged and excused.

Ouachita Corrections phone records

Donna Parks, an IT employee at the Ouachita Correctional Center, testified about the facility’s inmate phone system during the period Tellis was housed there in August 2015. The system flagged 13 calls from Tellis’s pod as possible three-way calls, which are often attempts by an inmate to connect outside parties to a monitored call to avoid detection.

The reason for this is that Eric Hill had testified that Tellis had called him on a three-way call after he had been arrested and said, “You’d better put this on someone else or I’ll F- you up.” This was possibly because Hill testified that Tellis had bragged to him that he had tortured an Asian woman to death for her PIN number to her debit card.

None of the three-way calls were logged under Tellis’s PIN number, Parks said, but she acknowledged that inmates routinely use each other’s PINs, making it impossible to identify or retrieve calls made under another inmate’s number.

Defense Attorney Bob Noel pushed hard against this, asking why the corrections staff couldn’t have caught the three-way call. Jones asked Parks if it would have taken listening to “all the calls” to find that, which Parks confirmed.

The defense pushes back

On cross-examination of Cookson, Noel focused on what the investigation did not find. No DNA belonging to Tellis was recovered from Hsiao’s home. No blood was found in his car. No blood-stained items were seized from his residence or Mahrous’s. He also drew out that Detective Jerry Kent had told Tellis during the August 11th interview that investigators would find his DNA in the bathroom, a statement Cookson acknowledged could be seen as a deliberate falsehood since they didn’t know anything about DNA in the bathroom, a standard tactic in the Reid Technique of interrogation.

On redirect, Jones returned to the bathroom, where Cookson said he observed what appeared to be faint blood on the wall. That blood was tested but produced only a partial DNA profile that could not be fully developed. Jones also noted that if a person had worn gloves no transfer evidence would be expected, and that Tellis had nearly two weeks between the murder and his first interview during which investigators had no knowledge of his movements.

With Cookson’s testimony concluded, the state rested its case. The defense rested without calling additional witnesses. Closing arguments are scheduled for Thursday before Judge Larry Jefferson, though whether he will issue a ruling that same day remains unclear.

CORINTH – After nearly two years at the Corinth-Alcorn Animal Shelter, Asher has been adopted.

The shelter said Asher spent 653 days in its care before officially finding a forever home.

According to the shelter, Asher was one of 28 dogs rescued from a cruelty case two summers ago. He arrived at the shelter July 30, 2024, scared and uncertain after enduring difficult conditions.

Asher was adopted by Grady, a shelter volunteer who chose to make him part of his family.

The shelter thanked Grady for giving Asher a home and said dogs like Asher are a reminder of why staff, volunteers and supporters continue their work.

The release is scheduled for 1:30 p.m. in front of Edgewater Mall.

The event comes as IMMS recognizes Endangered Species Day and highlights its work with Kemp’s ridley sea turtles, the most endangered species of sea turtle.

IMMS said the Mississippi Sound is an important habitat for Kemp’s ridley sea turtles, especially juveniles that often come into the organization’s care.

Officials said saving each turtle helps support the species’ population.

The Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks held its annual Fallen Officer Memorial Service on Thursday, honoring conservation officers who died in the line of duty while protecting Mississippi’s people and natural resources.

The ceremony, held during National Police Week, included remarks from MDWFP Executive Director Lynn Posey and a keynote address and wreath-laying ceremony led by Bill Kinkade, chairman of the House Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks Committee.

“Each year, we gather to remember and honor the brave men and women who gave their lives in the line of duty protecting Mississippi’s people and natural resources,” Posey said in a statement. “This memorial service, taking place during National Police Week, is a reminder of the risks officers face every day and the unwavering commitment they bring to their work.”

Since 1948, 12 MDWFP conservation officers have died in the line of duty. The agency erected its Fallen Officer Memorial in 2007 at the department’s Jackson office as a permanent tribute to those officers.

MDWFP officials said the memorial serves as a lasting tribute to officers who made the ultimate sacrifice while serving Mississippi’s citizens and conserving the state’s wildlife and natural resources.

JACKSON – The Mississippi State Department of Health has launched a statewide program aimed at expanding access to substance use disorder treatment across all 82 counties.

MSDH said the program is designed to identify risk earlier, reduce barriers to treatment and bring support closer to where patients live.

“This work reflects a simple principle: Substance use disorder care should be available earlier, closer to home, and as part of normal health care, not only after a person reaches crisis,” said Dr. Dan Edney, MSDH executive director and state health officer.

The program uses Epic, MSDH’s electronic health record system, and MyChart to help with screening, intervention and follow-up. Across all 84 MSDH clinics, patients complete an annual screening through MyChart before their visit or on a tablet when they arrive.

MSDH officials said the goal is to help clinicians meet patients at different levels of risk. Patients with low-risk screening results receive positive reinforcement, while clinicians receive guidance through Epic as screening results show greater risk.

Following a six-county pilot program, every county in Mississippi is now using the program. Patients who screen at high risk typically receive follow-up care from addiction specialists through video visits, reducing the need for travel.

MSDH said the program is especially important in Mississippi, where many residents face barriers to care, including transportation challenges, provider shortages and limited access to mental health and substance use treatment.

According to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, about 327,000 Mississippians ages 12 and older who needed substance use treatment did not receive it, based on 2022-2023 annual averages.

MSDH said it is one of the few state health departments in the country to provide direct, clinic-based substance use disorder treatment.

Officials said the agency is also exploring ways to safely extend care into the home for eligible patients as more people successfully engage in treatment.

JACKSON — A Jackson man was arrested Saturday after an exchange of gunfire damaged three vehicles during an altercation on Briarwood Drive, according to the Jackson Police Department.

Officers responded May 16 to the 400 block of Briarwood Drive for reports of shots fired.

Police said officers arrived and detained a Black man who had exited a vehicle while holding a firearm and was involved in a verbal altercation with a White male.

Investigators said the confrontation escalated into an exchange of gunfire, damaging three occupied vehicles. No injuries were reported.

Using surveillance footage, officers identified the suspect as 26-year-old DeMarcus Griffin. He was taken into custody at the scene, transported to the Jackson Police Department and later charged with three counts of shooting into occupied vehicles.

Police said the unidentified White male involved in the altercation fled the scene.

The investigation remains ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the Jackson Police Department at 601-960-1604 or Crime Stoppers at 601-355-TIPS (8477). Authorities said tipsters could receive up to $2,500 if their information leads to an arrest.

HERNANDO — A Memphis man who had been a fugitive for eight years was sentenced Thursday to more than seven years in federal prison after authorities found him in possession of seven firearms during a traffic stop in Hernando, federal officials said.

Keon J. Carwell, 39, of Memphis, Tennessee, was sentenced to 87 months in prison followed by three years of supervised release after pleading guilty to possession of firearms by a convicted felon.

According to prosecutors, officers with the Hernando Police Department stopped a vehicle March 31, 2024, in which Carwell was riding. During the investigation, officers confirmed Carwell was wanted on an active federal warrant stemming from a 2016 gun charge in Tennessee.

Authorities said Carwell was found with seven firearms, including a pistol reported stolen during a burglary at a federally licensed firearms dealer, a rifle with an obliterated serial number and a sawed-off shotgun. Six of the firearms were loaded.

Senior U.S. District Judge Michael P. Mills handed down the sentence in federal court in Oxford.

Scott F. Leary, U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Mississippi, praised Hernando police and federal agents involved in the case.

“The Hernando Police Department conducted an investigation and apprehended a man that had been a fugitive for eight years,” Leary said in a statement. “A community is safer today as a result of their hard work.”

Joshua Jackson, special agent in charge for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives in New Orleans, said the case reflects ongoing efforts to target violent gun crime.

“In our effort to disrupt violent gun crime in our community, ATF will continue to focus efforts on prohibited individuals who unlawfully possess firearms,” Jackson said.

The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and Hernando Police Department investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Julie Addison prosecuted the matter.

Federal officials said the case was part of Project Safe Neighborhoods, a nationwide initiative aimed at reducing violent crime and gun violence.

FLOWOOD — Flowood will officially unveil and adopt its first municipal flag Monday evening during the city’s regularly scheduled Board of Aldermen meeting at City Hall.

The ceremony is set for 6 p.m. at Flowood City Hall, located at 2101 Airport Road, and marks the first time the city has formally adopted an official flag since incorporating in 1989.

City leaders said the flag was chosen through a student design competition launched earlier this year under the direction of Mayor Kathy Smith. Students from Hartfield Academy, Jackson Preparatory School and Northwest Rankin High School were invited to submit designs representing the character and identity of the city.

Officials said 42 entries were submitted for consideration. The winning design was created by Rodgers Brown, a 10th grade student at Northwest Rankin High School.

During the ceremony, the city will recognize Brown and his art teacher, Mandy Brownlee, for their contributions. Brown will receive a $1,000 scholarship from the city, while Brownlee will receive a $200 donation for art supplies from Pacesetter Gallery in support of arts education.

City officials described the unveiling as a historic milestone celebrating civic pride and community identity. Members of the public are invited to attend.

GREENVILLE – Four women were arrested Friday after Greenville police executed a search warrant as part of an ongoing narcotics investigation.

The Greenville Police Department said members of its Special Response Team and Special Operations Unit executed the court-authorized search warrant around 8:37 a.m. May 15 at a residence on Wallstreet Lane.

Police said officers announced their presence but did not receive a response before entering the home. Four adult women inside the residence were safely detained while officers secured the home and conducted a search.

During the search, investigators said they recovered suspected methamphetamine, drug paraphernalia, syringes, digital scales, packaging materials and other items commonly associated with illegal narcotics activity.

Tia Spencer was charged with possession of drug paraphernalia.

HATTIESBURG — It’s been more than 42 years since Deborah Faye Owens allegedly stepped out of her husband’s vehicle into nowhere on a New Year’s morning.

Investigators still have no answers about what happened to the 27-year-old woman after she and her husband left a New Year’s Eve celebration in the early hours of Jan. 1, 1984.

According to the Hattiesburg Police Department, Owens was last seen after attending the party with her husband. Authorities said the couple allegedly got into an argument while driving home, and her husband told investigators that Owens asked to be let out of the vehicle.

He told police he pulled over and let her out, then drove away. Owens has not been seen or heard from since.

Owens was a white female, and at the time of her disappearance, she was 27 years old.

A 1985 report in The Clarion-Ledger quoted Hattiesburg Detective Bob Hopkins as saying that Owens’ disappearance was unusual because she had always remained in contact with family or friends in the past.

“It’s not the first time she’s done something like this, but it’s the first time she hasn’t contacted anyone,” Hopkins told the newspaper.

In the months after Owens vanished, local newspapers published classified legal notices in April 1984 seeking a divorce from “Deborah Faye Owens, whose last known address was Hattiesburg, Mississippi but whose present residence and address is unknown,” citing cruel and unusual treatment.

Little additional information about the case was publicly released in the years that followed. Owens’ name appeared briefly in a 1987 Clarion-Ledger story about unresolved missing persons cases in Mississippi, but no major developments have ever been announced.

Today, Owens’ disappearance remains unsolved.

Anyone with information about Deborah Faye Owens or her disappearance is asked to contact the Hattiesburg Police Department at (601) 545-4971.

JACKSON — Attorney General Lynn Fitch announced the launch of Operation Hope on Monday, a new multi-agency initiative aimed at locating missing foster children, with authorities saying 13 children were found and brought to safety during the operation.

Fitch joined U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Administration for Children and Families Assistant Secretary Alex J. Adams, HHS Inspector General T. March Bell and Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services Commissioner Andrea Sanders to announce the program.

Officials said the operation combined law enforcement, child welfare agencies and support services in an effort to locate vulnerable children in foster care before they could be exploited or harmed.

“We are proud to have helped kick off this program here in Mississippi,” Fitch said. “Over the past several weeks of planning and in the execution of the operation last week, it was always our intention not only to locate vulnerable Mississippi youth but also to create a model that can be used in other states.”

Fitch said the effort was designed to show children “that they matter, and that they deserve hope.”

Adams said the operation recovered 87% of the missing foster youth identified during the initiative in less than 48 hours.

“To continue serving the best interests of children, Operation Hope will be replicated in other states, and we will leave no stone unturned when searching for these kids,” Adams said.

Bell, the HHS inspector general, said missing foster children require “a rapid, multi-faceted law enforcement response” and called the Mississippi effort a model for other states.

Sanders, commissioner of the Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services, said the operation focused on ensuring vulnerable children knew “someone was looking for them.”

“Every child located through this operation represents a young person who matters deeply and deserves safety, support, and hope for the future,” Sanders said.

Officials said children located during the operation were offered support services in addition to being recovered safely.

According to the announcement, the federal government first launched a similar initiative known as Project Hope in Kansas and Missouri, where officials said 42 missing children were located.

FLORENCE — Alex Cooper, a longtime Florence school bus driver and beloved local Santa Claus known to generations of families across Rankin County and the state, has died after suffering critical injuries in a school bus crash earlier this month.

Cooper, known affectionately throughout the community as “Buddy,” died Saturday, May 16, according to a Facebook post from his son, Gabe Cooper.

“My dad went home to be with Jesus today,” Gabe Cooper wrote. “I want to deeply thank the support system the family has had throughout this ordeal.”

The crash happened May 11 on Highway 49 near Eagle Post Road in Florence when an 18-wheeler struck a Rankin County school bus head-on, according to authorities. Cooper was driving the bus at the time. Family members said the brakes on the 18-wheeler went out.

Officials said there were no students on the bus during the crash.

Cooper, 79, suffered catastrophic injuries and was rushed to the hospital in critical condition. Family members later said he was paralyzed from the neck down and battling internal injuries following the wreck.

In a fundraising campaign created after the crash, Gabe Cooper described his father as a man who spent decades serving the community both behind the wheel of a school bus and as a familiar face during the Christmas season.

“For years, he has brought joy to children and families as Santa Claus during the Christmas season,” the fundraiser said. “Whether driving a school bus, lending a helping hand, or making children smile in a Santa suit, he has spent his life serving others and loving this community well.”

In the days following the crash, social media filled with tributes from former students, parents and community members sharing memories of Cooper’s kindness and generosity.

Beyond driving a school bus, Cooper became widely known across Mississippi for portraying Santa Claus at community events, shopping malls, parades, and official holiday celebrations. In a previous interview with Darkhorse Press during a Christmas event, Cooper reflected on one of his proudest moments as Santa.

“The crowning achievement of my term as Santa is being Santa for the Governor, the First Lady, and you, the people of Mississippi,” Cooper said.

The Florence Police Department investigated the crash.

Gabe Cooper said the family plans to announce details for a celebration of life at a later time. In lieu of flowers, the family requested donations be made to The Little Lighthouse.

Editor’s note: Buddy Cooper was a friend and a dear brother in Christ. Our deepest condolences to his family. The light he brought to our lives and especially our Christmases will never go out.

STARKVILLE — Since 1926, Mississippi State’s Orientation sessions have offered new Bulldogs a warm welcome. As MSU Orientation marks 100 years, an exhibit highlighting the program’s history is opening in the Colvard Student Union Art Gallery.

“It’s a special year to be able to look back over the past century. While times have changed, the main goals have remained constant—welcoming students, easing their anxieties as they enroll, assisting with their class schedules and providing helpful information,” said Director of Orientation and Events Jake Hartfield.

The “100 Years of Orientation at Mississippi State” exhibit, located on the Union’s second floor, is open throughout the summer. A come-and-go reception will be held May 29, 3:30-5 p.m., and Hartfield encouraged alumni, current and former administrators and everyone affiliated with the Orientation program, past or present, to mark the occasion and interact with current Orientation Leaders.

Students and their guests attending MSU Orientation sessions this summer also can view the exhibit, which includes photographs, pamphlets and even clothing items from past years. Orientation Leaders, or OLs as they are sometimes known, play a major role in hosting new students and their families, answering questions and shepherding students into university life.

Hartfield, who also served as an OL during his own student days at MSU, said the group has been a key part of setting the tone for Southern hospitality to newcomers since it formed in 1979.

“Each Orientation session is an all-hands-on-deck event. From our Orientation Leaders to our staff members, administrators and advisors, we want to roll out the maroon carpet for our new students, no matter if it’s the first or the last session. We want to ensure that everybody’s getting the same exciting, high-energy experience,” Hartfield said.

With over 5,000 incoming students attending summer Orientation, the program hosts more than 10,000 total, including parents and other guests, across approximately 15 sessions. MSU President Mark E. Keenum has attended Orientation throughout his tenure, and each event includes a variety of university speakers, panels, ice cream socials and the iconic MSU Orientation original skit, which pays homage each year to a distinctive part of student life.

“It takes a lot of energy and a servant’s heart to provide the best experience possible. We want to make sure our new students have the resources they need to feel they’re in good hands, prepared and that they made the right choice in choosing Mississippi State,” Hartfield said.

To further mark the 100-year milestone, university leaders are planning a fall tailgate for current and former Orientation Leaders, administrators and staff. The MSU Foundation also has an MSU Orientation Leaders Excellence Fund available at www.dda.msstate.edu/give-now?f=313024 .

Incoming students can confirm their MSU enrollment by signing up for Orientation at www.orientation.msstate.edu .

The year was 1975. The Vietnam War was coming to a close, Microsoft had just been founded and Bruce Springsteen was topping the charts. South Central Regional Medical Center, which was called Jones County Community Hospital at the time, had just entered its third decade of faithfully serving the Pine Belt, and three young women joined the staff: Judy Hicks, Nell Warren and Jodie Mancil. Today, a half-century later, South Central Regional Medical Center wants to pause and celebrate the impact they have made on the organization.

Judy Hicks

Judy is a Laurel native who spent most of her adolescence living in Germany, France, Belgium and in various states across the eastern seaboard. Her father was in the Army, and moving was part of the job. When her father retired, the whole family moved back to Laurel, and Judy, who was 21 at the time, began working in admissions at Jones County Community Hospital in July 1975.

“I didn’t know what insurance was or what a policy was,” Judy said. “I was working from noon until 9 p.m., and I remember telling my dad, ‘I don’t like it. I want to quit.’ Then he said, ‘you have not been there long enough. Give it six months.’”

Judy did as her father suggested and to her surprise, she fell in love with the challenge of her work, devoting 50 years of her professional career to advocating for patients and navigating evolving regulations.

After two years of working in admissions, Judy was transferred to working in the insurance department. Judy recalls the adjustment to working in insurance as having been difficult.

Judy was later promoted to a supervisory role and eventually became Director of Patient Accounts. She served in this role until 2019 and now is in the process of training others to fill her shoes.

Judy’s devotion to her work is admirable, showing that persistence and gumption go a long way in creating a lasting career.

Nell Warren Nell is a Paulding native who graduated from South Side High School in Heidelberg.

She first began working in dietary at Jones County Community Hospital as a helper, where she prepped tube feeds for patients, worked in the dish room and worked in the food line.

“I have done pretty much everything except cook, I haven’t done any of that,” Nell said.

Today, Nell can be found in the physicians’ lounge at South Central Regional Medical Center, where she ensures that physicians are well taken care of nutritionally, while always offering a smile or words of encouragement.

“I love people,” Nell said. “I love being around people. I like to hug.”

Nell’s presence is a reminder that care is not only clinical, it is human.

Jodie Mancil

Jodie Mancil was born in Texas but lived abroad for thirteen years. Her father worked in the oil business and the company he worked for relocated her family to Sicily, Italy, and Tripoli, Libya. She even attended boarding school in Switzerland for a brief period, while her parents worked in Mozambique, Africa.

“My father asked to be transferred so that the family could be a unit again before my sister and I were grown and married; and they moved him from Africa to Soso, Mississippi,” Jodie said.

Jodie lived in the area and earned a bachelor’s degree in medical technology from the University of Southern Mississippi. She began working at Jones County Community Hospital in July 1975 as a medical technologist.

Throughout the years, she has become an integral member of the lab team. She has served as the blood bank supervisor for almost ten years, and in this role, she teaches students who come into the lab as part of their training.

“It is my calling from the Lord to teach, and I enjoy teaching,” Jodie said. “I enjoy helping others. If you look at it as a ministry, it is not a job. Some days are harder than others, but in the end the Lord has you here for a reason. I try to tell my students to bloom where they are planted, and I am planted here.”

Judy, Nell and Jodie’s stories teach us many lessons, but one lesson stands out among the rest — it is that perspective shapes purpose. For Judy, work brought fulfillment. For Nell, it brought connection. For Jodie, it became a mission field. When work is rooted in meaning, it becomes more than a job, it becomes a life calling.

STARKVILLE – A Starkville man has been charged after police said he entered a home, struck a woman with a bat and attempted to strangle her.

The Starkville Police Department said officers responded Sunday, May 17, around 11 a.m. to a report of an assault that had occurred earlier that day at a residence on Peoples Street.

Police said the victim was treated at Baptist Memorial Hospital-Oktibbeha County and later released.

Blair Bell, 35, of Starkville, was charged with domestic violence-aggravated assault and residential burglary. Police said Bell turned himself in Monday morning.

The incident remains under investigation.

According to the National Coalition Against Domestic Violence, 1 in 4 women and 1 in 7 men in the United States have experienced severe physical violence by an intimate partner during their lifetime.

Anyone with information about the incident or other criminal activity is asked to contact the Starkville Police Department at 662-323-4131, Golden Triangle Crime Stoppers at 800-530-7151, or submit an anonymous tip through the department’s website. Crime Stoppers may offer a cash reward.

HINDS COUNTY – Two men died after separate crashes involving off-road vehicles in Hinds County, according to Hinds County Coroner Jeramiah Howard.

The first crash happened Saturday, May 16, in the 3600 block of McFarland Road in Raymond.

Authorities said Timothy Bright, 59, of Jackson, was a passenger in a side-by-side that left the roadway and overturned. Bright died at the scene.

A second crash happened May 9 in the 1600 block of South Norrell Road in Bolton.

Authorities said Andy Sanders, 56, of Bolton, was driving an ATV that left the roadway and struck a tree. Sanders died from his injuries at a local hospital on Friday, May 15.

JACKSON – A man was arrested after Capitol Police said he led officers on a high-speed chase from Jackson to Crystal Springs early Wednesday morning.

Capitol Police officers attempted to stop a motorcycle traveling at a high rate of speed on Ridgewood Road around 5:39 a.m., according to PIO, Bailey C. Martin.

Authorities said the motorcycle fled from officers, leading them through multiple roads and onto Interstate 55 South at speeds exceeding 140 mph.

The pursuit continued into Crystal Springs, where the driver was identified as Kyle King, 33. King was taken into custody on Ruby Road with assistance from the Copiah County Sheriff’s Office.

King is charged with felony fleeing and possession of paraphernalia involving methamphetamine. Authorities said he also had warrants from other surrounding jurisdictions.

No additional information was immediately released.
